html:
A court-like body set up in South Africa in 1996 to face the crimes of apartheid. The government of Nelson Mandela created it, and Archbishop Desmond Tutu chaired it.

Victims of killing, torture and abduction from 1960 to 1994 gave statements, and some told their stories at public hearings in town halls and churches, broadcast on radio and television. Perpetrators, from police officers to liberation fighters, could ask for amnesty. They got it only if they told the whole truth and showed the crime had a political motive. About 7,000 applied, and most were refused.

The idea was restorative justice: a full public record in place of trials, so that a divided country could live together. Critics said victims got little money and many senior officials never came forward. The final report came out in 1998. The commission became a model for truth commissions in Sierra Leone, Liberia and other countries, while Rwanda dealt with its genocide through the very different gacaca courts.
sum: A court-like body set up in South Africa in 1996 to face the crimes of apartheid. The government of Nelson Mandela created it, and Archbishop Desmond Tutu chaired it.
